description: We are Team G.O.A.T (Goal Oriented Astronautics Team).
summary:
Bobcat Valley is an interactive web app for tracking land subsidence in California’s Central Valley. Users drag a box over any area, pick two dates, and see how far the ground sank or rose. Clicking a spot charts its history alongside nearby groundwater wells, rainfall and soil moisture.
For the "Dancing With the SARS" challenge, we built a pipeline that turns raw NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) radar data into ground-movement measurements. It reads 125 L-band interferograms covering the valley, every 12 days from November 2025 to October 2026. It shows NISAR beside California Department of Water Resources’ Sentinel-1 record from 2015, checks the two against each other, and adds NISAR soil moisture and NASA POWER precipitation. M.E.R.L.I.N. (Machine Earth Resources Learning Intelligence Network) is our machine-learning model that forecasts the next six months of sinking from radar history and groundwater levels. On held-out 2025–2026 data, it was about twice as accurate as repeating the recent trend.
This issue matters because most Central Valley land subsidence is permanent; the aquifer loses storage it never regains. Sinking land also damages canals like the California Aqueduct, which carries water to millions of Californians, so we integrated a system that flags the canal stretches at risk as well.
details: BobcatValley is a free web app for tracking land subsidence in California's Central Valley. Users draw a box on a satellite map, pick two dates, and see the ground colored by how far it sank or rose, with layers for rivers, cities, groundwater wells, rainfall and soil moisture. Clicking a spot charts its history and a six-month forecast from our M.E.R.L.I.N. machine-learning model, and California Aqueduct segments are flagged where sinking crosses set thresholds. We built a Python pipeline that streams only the needed layers of 125 NASA-ISRO NISAR radar files, converts radar phase into centimeters of movement, and checks it against California DWR's Sentinel-1 record. The app uses Streamlit, Leaflet, Plotly, NumPy, pandas, h5py and scikit-learn, and runs on an ordinary laptop. Its Windows XP design and hand-drawn team artwork give it a human element and is built to be intuitive and nostalgic. We focused on honesty, labeling measurements separately from forecasts and showing NISAR's uncertainty. Because most subsidence is permanent and damages canals that supply millions of Californians, we want farmers, residents and water agencies to see where the ground is sinking and act sooner.
